Question #1: Run 17 / 5, 17 %% 5, and 17 %/% 5 side by side. In your own words, explain how these three results relate to each other mathematically.
```{r}
a <- 17
b <- 5
a / b
a %% b
a %/% b
```
Answer: the first one is a simple division, the second is modulo, the third result is the whole-number (integer) division. They relate mathematically by being in the category of division.

Question #2: Predict the output of 10 %% 3 and 10 %/% 3 before running the code. Were you correct? If not, explain what you misunderstood.

```{r}
a <- 10
b <- 3 
a %% b : 1
a %/% b : 3

```
Answer: Yes, my prediction was correct.

PART B

```{r}
# TODO: Use typeof() to check the type of each of x, y, z, w, v
x <- 42
y <- 42L        # the L suffix forces an integer
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i     # complex number

typeof(x <- 42)
typeof(y <- 42L)
typeof(z <- "42")
typeof(w <- TRUE)
typeof(v <- 3 + 2i)



```
```{r}
# TODO: Use class() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
class(x <- 42)
class(y <- 42L)        
class(z <- "42")
class(w <- TRUE)
class(v <- 3 + 2i) 
```
```{r}
# TODO: Use mode() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
mode(x <- 42)
mode(y <- 42L)
mode(z <- "42")
mode(w <- TRUE)
mode(v <- 3 + 2i)
```
Question #3): x <- 42 and y <- 42L look almost identical, but typeof(x) and typeof(y) give different answers. Explain the difference in your own words.

```{r}
typeof(x <- 42)
typeof(y <- 42L)
```
Answer: It is identical but it differs because "L" suffix forces an integer.

Question #4: Is typeof() ever different from class() and from mode() for the same object? Look at your results above and explain any case where this happens (or, if you did not see one, explain what you would expect for a matrix or factor).

Answer: typeof() reports the low-level storage type; class() reports the object’s class, which is sometimes more general

Question #5: When you ran the conversion-fail chunk, R produced NA and a warning instead of stopping with an error.

Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?

Answer: R is designed to handle conversion errors safely so the program can continue running instead of stopping completely.

What are the risks of this behavior if you don’t read your warnings?

Answer: Invalid values may become NA, causing incorrect calculations and results without us noticing the problem.

Question #6: 

```{r}
#What do as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1) produce?
as.logical(2)
as.logical(-1)
```
Test it, then explain the rule R seems to be following.

Answer: R converts 0 to FALSE and any nonzero number, wheter positive or negative, to TRUE.

Question #7: 

Answer: paste() and paste0() produced different results for the same two strings. Explain exactly why, referencing what each function does by default.

paste() uses a space as the default separator between strings, while paste0() uses no separator. That is why their results are different.

Question #8

Answer: No, it did not cause an error. paste0() automatically converts numeric values such as age into character strings when combining them with text. This relates to Part C because R can convert values from one data type to another using conversion functions.

Aswer: An error occurs because "5" is a character string, while 5 is numeric.

```{r}
as.numeric("5") + 5
```

Question #9

Answer: R requires explicit conversion because character strings and numbers are different data types. This helps prevent unexpected results and makes the programmer specify when text should be treated as a number.

Question #10

Answer: The column probably contains character values instead of numeric values, possibly because the file was imported as text or contains nonnumeric characters. I would use typeof(), class(), and str() to check its data type and inspect the values for unwanted characters. Then I would use as.numeric() to convert the column into numbers. I would also check for warnings and NA values before using sum().

Conclusion

Answer: I learned that R uses different data types, such as numeric, character, and logical. The functions typeof(), class(), and mode() help identify the type of a value. Conversion functions such as as.numeric() and as.logical() change values between types. Understanding data types helps prevent errors when performing calculations or combining data.
